concepts.title: Splitting Numbers with Floor Division and Modulus

questions.q: Using the method 'Splitting Numbers with Floor Division and Modulus', work with: number = 2048. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of two_digit_total.
Take the relation taught for 'Splitting Numbers with Floor Division and Modulus' and work with: number = 8192. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of two_digit_total.
Explain in your own words what 'Splitting Numbers with Floor Division and Modulus' refers to.
questions.a: Floor division (//) keeps only the whole part of a quotient, while modulus (%) keeps only the remainder; together they split a number into its digits, since the last digit is the remainder on division by 10 and the rest is the floor quotient.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Splitting Numbers with Floor Division and Modulus'.
questions.a: Dividing by 10 with // drops the final digit, and taking % 10 keeps it.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Splitting Numbers with Floor Division and Modulus', in plain ASCII form.

Evaluate 20 + 30 * 40 the way Python does, showing each step.. Use the method 'Operator Precedence in Expressions'. Work with: a = 200, b = 24, c = 500. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of value.

Evaluate 15.0 / 4 + (8 + 3.0) step by step.. Use the method 'Operator Precedence in Expressions'. Work with: a = 15, b = 5, c = 100. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of value.
Explain in your own words what 'Operator Precedence in Expressions' refers to.
questions.a: Python evaluates an expression by applying operators in order of precedence: exponentiation first, then unary signs, then multiply-divide-modulus, then add-subtract, with equal-precedence operators working left to right and parentheses overriding everything.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Operator Precedence in Expressions'.
questions.a: Parentheses beat every rule, so adding them is how you force a different evaluation order.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Operator Precedence in Expressions', in plain ASCII form.
Using the method 'Logical Errors and Debugging', work with: first = 60, second = 6. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of gap.
Take the relation taught for 'Logical Errors and Debugging' and work with: first = 400, second = 3. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of gap.
Explain in your own words what 'Logical Errors and Debugging' refers to.
questions.a: A logical (semantic) error lets a program run to completion but prints wrong results, unlike a syntax error which stops execution and a runtime error which aborts a running program, for example division by zero.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Logical Errors and Debugging'.
questions.a: The only clue to a logical error is output that looks plausible but is wrong, so work backwards from the result.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Logical Errors and Debugging', in plain ASCII form.
Using the method 'Simple Interest and Amount Payable', work with: principal = 5000, rate = 10, years = 1500. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of amount.
Take the relation taught for 'Simple Interest and Amount Payable' and work with: principal = 1200, rate = 12, years = 200. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of amount.
Explain in your own words what 'Simple Interest and Amount Payable' refers to.
questions.a: Money lent at simple interest grows by principal times rate times years divided by 100, and the amount to repay is the principal plus that interest.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Simple Interest and Amount Payable'.
questions.a: Simple interest accrues on the original principal alone, never on accumulated interest.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Simple Interest and Amount Payable', in plain ASCII form.
Using the method 'Celsius to Fahrenheit Conversion', work with: celsius = 30. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of fahrenheit.
Take the relation taught for 'Celsius to Fahrenheit Conversion' and work with: celsius = 30. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of fahrenheit.
Explain in your own words what 'Celsius to Fahrenheit Conversion' refers to.
questions.a: A Celsius temperature converts to Fahrenheit by scaling it by nine-fifths and shifting by 32 degrees; water boils at 100 C, which maps to 212 F, and freezes at 0 C, mapping to 32 F.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Celsius to Fahrenheit Conversion'.
questions.a: Multiply by 9/5 first, then add 32; reversing the order gives a wrong scale.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Celsius to Fahrenheit Conversion', in plain ASCII form.

Compute the volume of a sphere of radius 7 cm using 4/3 pi r cubed.. Use the method 'Volume of a Sphere'. Work with: radius = 40. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of volume.
Find the volume of spheres with radii 12 cm and 16 cm.. Use the method 'Volume of a Sphere'. Work with: radius = 60. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of volume.
Explain in your own words what 'Volume of a Sphere' refers to.
questions.a: A sphere of radius r fills four-thirds of pi times the cube of its radius, so the volume program cubes the radius with the ** operator and multiplies by 4/3 and pi.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Volume of a Sphere'.
questions.a: Exponentiation has the highest precedence, so radius ** 3 is evaluated before any multiplication.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Volume of a Sphere', in plain ASCII form.

concepts.title: The String Trap of the input Function

questions.q: Using the method 'The String Trap of the input Function', work with: digit = 5. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of true_double.
Take the relation taught for 'The String Trap of the input Function' and work with: digit = 75. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of true_double.
Explain in your own words what 'The String Trap of the input Function' refers to.
questions.a: The input() function always hands back a string, so doubling a captured '2' with * repeats the text instead of doubling the number; explicit conversion with int() before multiplying gives the numeric answer.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The String Trap of the input Function'.
questions.a: Everything typed at the keyboard arrives as text, so cast it with int() or float() before arithmetic.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'The String Trap of the input Function', in plain ASCII form.
Explain in your own words what 'Identifier Naming Rules and Keywords' refers to.
questions.a: An identifier names a variable or function: it must start with a letter or underscore, may continue with letters, digits or underscores, cannot contain special symbols or spaces, and must never clash with a reserved keyword such as True or class.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Identifier Naming Rules and Keywords'.
questions.a: Python is case-sensitive, so Total, total and TOTAL name three different variables.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Identifier Naming Rules and Keywords', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: valid(name) = starts with letter or _ and no keyword
